en: Om. Salutations to the venerable gurus;
salutations to the illustrious Sundaragaṇapati.

Vātulāgama, Jñānapūjā — Re 47827 1) Knowledge is twofold. Now, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the worship of knowledge: "Next, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the worship of knowledge" (I.4b).
How does knowledge, which is exceedingly difficult to attain, arise in men?
Knowledge, however, should be understood as twofold, through the distinction between the higher (para) and the lower (apara).
Of these, the first is the supreme knowledge, which is the vision of the Lord, the fetter, and the self.
The second is the lower knowledge (aparajñāna), which consists solely in the perception of fetters;
it is like the difference observed at night between the eyes of a man and those of a cat.
Thus is the characteristic of knowledge; such is this higher and lower [knowledge].
Whatever karma one has performed in another birth, through the particularity of its ripening—

2) Authority (adhikāra): By the glance of the Knowledge-Teacher (jñānācārya), the wise one who knows the three categories and the means of valid cognition, having attained knowledge of the objects of knowledge through that knowledge, is entitled to the rites of the worship of knowledge and so forth. (I.5a)
3) Nitya-karma:
Having risen early in the morning, one should contemplate Śiva for the sake of steadfastness;
then, one should commence the daily rites according to the prescriptions of the ritual section (kriyākāṇḍa).
At the time of bathing, having meditated upon the water as an ocean of supreme nectar,
one should remember Śiva himself— partless, stainless, and eternally liberated.
Having bathed and being joined with Vedic rites, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana);
one should contemplate the Doer, the imperishable witness of all actions.

4) Ācamanādi (Rinsing the Mouth, etc.): One should rinse the mouth with mantras beginning with the *ātmatattva* and ending with *śiva*. Having realized [the self] as the supreme light, one should wear the sacred ash while reciting the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*).
One should perform the rite either by means of smearing [the body with ashes] or by the method of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). (5) Prāṇāyāma:
One should perform prāṇāyāma with the root mantra; through exhalation (recaka), it destroys sin.
Having filled [the vessel] with that auspicious merit and performed the *kumbhaka* breath-retention,
one should then perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and thereafter the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
One should meditate upon Śiva, who is both with parts and without parts, eternal, and the bliss of consciousness.
6) Tarpaṇa (Libation): Having meditated upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should offer three handfuls of water for honor (arghya) while reciting the root mantra.
One should perform the libation for one's own lineage-guru through the path of the lineage,
as well as the libation for the Samaya-gurus and the [deity] forms according to the rules;
one should offer the *arghya* with their respective personal-name mantras and with the mantra of Śiva.
One should offer libations with that water in the same sequence, ending with "svāhā";
then, having sprinkled oneself with the root mantra and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one becomes fully consecrated (sakalīkṛta).
7) Śivalaya-darśana (Beholding the Temple of Śiva): Having meditated upon Śiva, one should then show him the temple and its surroundings. 8) Pūjāsthāna-praveśana (Entering the Place of Worship).
Having washed his feet and sipped water, he should enter the place of worship.
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat,
having applied sacred ash, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and the limbs.
Having presented the *arghya* everywhere and having performed purification especially thoroughly,
one should bathe the Supreme Lord after worshipping Him according to the prescribed rite.
9) Niṣṭhā: One should likewise remain established in samādhi until midday;
[one perceives] the Liṅga consisting of the light of knowledge, blazing intensely like the bright moon.
One should fix the mind and the vital breaths there, situated between the eyebrows; absorbed in that and becoming one with it, the yogi should gradually lead the consciousness into emptiness.
When the mind has perished, the supreme bliss of consciousness (cidānanda) shines forth by itself;
this is indeed described as samādhi, the abode of the qualities such as aṇimā and the rest.
If one is unable to do this, then, having meditated upon Śiva and the others,
one should [recite] the Śiva-mantra through the limbs (pratīka) and so forth, according to the path taught by the Guru.
In its absence, having performed recitation and listened to the scriptures with devotion,
the teacher of knowledge should then begin the midday worship.
10) Jñānapūjā: Taking recourse to the southern gate, one should perform the worship of knowledge (jñānapūjā).
Worship of the South is preeminent; it is the cause for attaining the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Assuming the form of the Teacher and facing southward,
Hara should provide instruction in knowledge for the sake of destroying the bonds of bound souls (paśus).
Therefore, the worship of the southern face shall be endowed with knowledge;
having commenced the worship there, one should indeed perform the application of sacred ash.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord;
having recited the five-syllabled mantra once and made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should offer the arghya with those waters.
One should sprinkle the collection of materials at the entrance and other places with the Śiva-mantra.

Having placed a rosary in the southeast and a vessel for ashes in the southwest,
and having placed the Śiva-śāstra in the west, he should then perform worship.
One should thoroughly honor the foremost among the devotees of Śiva from the north;
having prostrated and requested them to bear witness to the worship, one should meditate upon Śiva.
12) Bhūtaśuddhi:

Having purified the self and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate with hands joined in añjali upon [the Self] as conjoined with the tattvas and upatattvas, characterized by both the gross and the subtle. (I.7a)
One should contemplate the body and the embodied soul as distinct within this body joined with the paths,
and likewise remember each triad of principles beginning with earth individually.
Having meditated upon the activity of Śiva’s command, he became a recipient of the fruits of his past karma;
yet that [karma] was destroyed within his body by his own will, just as it was through discernment.
Just as one who has left an old house and reached a new one, so too,
having abandoned the body, he entered the abode of Śiva where divine splendor flourishes.

One should contemplate that one has indeed attained the eternal state consisting of consciousness and bliss. 13) Inner Sacrifice (Antaryāga): Having bathed one's own body with nectar and being permeated by the agitated Śakti.
One should contemplate the self, situated within that abode, as having the form of Śiva— a body consisting of the abode of Śiva and a profuse stream of nectar.
Therefore, the internal sacrifice should be performed within the pure self;
one should offer the partless, all-pervading Śiva as an oblation in the sky between the eyebrows.
One should contemplate the place of worship as pure knowledge, whose nature is reality;
having dispelled the web of bonds with divine vision through the splendor of Śiva. (I.7b)
14) Purity of the Substance (dravyaśuddhi): One should visualize the arghya vessel as completely filled by means of the Astra-mantra alone;
having washed it with the Bahurūpa-mantra and with the Śiva-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water and arrange perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should worship it eleven times with the five-syllabled mantra.
Having performed the binding of the directions and other rites, one should consecrate the collection of materials with the Dhenu-mudrā to render them nectar-like,
sprinkle them, and purify them through the rites of inspection and so forth.
One should recite the Śiva-mantra ten times over the flowers;
for one whose mantra has been purified, this should be preceded by three claps of the hands.
Having performed the protection of the directions and so forth, one should contemplate the place as flooded with nectar and filled with the splendor of Śiva, both internally and externally.
Taking the *liṅga* with the root mantra, one should discard the stale flower;
having consecrated it with the weapon mantra, one should sprinkle it with the previously offered water of honor (*arghya*).
In that [seat], one should worship with the seat-mantra and the form-mantra;
having invoked Śiva with the root-mantra, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having offered incense and a lamp from the heart-mantra, one should present the arghya with the root-mantra;
having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth.
Having bathed Śiva with perfumed water, pure water, and arghya-water consecrated with the root mantra,
one should wipe him with a clean cloth and place him upon a seat.
Having placed drops of ash, flowers, and *arghya*, one should offer them;
(15) beginning with worship— (15) *arcanādi*—
one should contemplate the form of the seat ending in *Kuṭilā*, which consists of the nature of will, knowledge, and action.
Having meditated upon Lagulīśvara as identical with Śiva through the root mantra,
one should again worship him with the seat and the [two] forms using the root mantra itself.
Having meditated upon Śiva, who is consciousness-bliss, eternally manifest and imperishable,
[one should place him] in the two feet consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and in the two faces consisting of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
One should offer the triad beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) at the top of the head, which consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);
and one should worship Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and garlands.
Having seen the bull in front and the lords of sages on both sides, [one should worship them].
Having worshipped Agastya and the others, one should then worship one's own guru.
Having offered incense and a lamp to Śiva, and having presented three handfuls of flowers,
one should cause him to be given the evening meal, endowed with the six flavors and accompanied by side dishes.
Having offered water for drinking and sipping, one should cause betel-leaf to be presented;
then, having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should worship Śiva until the conclusion of the recitation.
Having praised Mahādeva with hymns and having bowed down again and again with devotion,
one should cause the entire fruit of that worship to be conveyed by means of water.
One should pray for one's desired object there and worship Śiva with flowers. (11) Having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* to him, [one should worship] the Supreme Lord with the root mantra.
Having meditated upon the partless and stainless [deity], one should seat it in its proper place;
having worshipped, praised, and bowed to one's own guru upon the seat, one should dismiss him.
One should contemplate Śiva— the supreme auspiciousness, partless, stainless, radiant,
consisting of consciousness and bliss, eternal, and whose form is splendor.
One should consume his food offering; no such thing as "nirmālya" exists for him.
In this way, the wise man performs worship endowed with knowledge.
Right here he becomes wealthy and glorious, and in the end, he shall attain liberation.
